title: The mobile visit for a consumer brand
metaTitle: The phone visit for a brand shop
excerpt: Shoppers will judge a brand on a phone. The first screen still has to show the object clearly and offer a way to see the product. Design that width first.
alt: Three pale speckled bottles on a gray surface, two holding dried seed heads. Objects set out to be identified, which is the first job of a phone screen.
caption: Three pale speckled bottles on a gray surface, two holding dried seed heads. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What has to be on the first phone screen?
faqs.answer: The object, large enough to name, one plain sentence, and a thumb-sized link to the product. If the link slips below the first view, the page is a poster. Design this screen before the wide crop gets a vote.

faqs.question: Which speed targets apply to a product hero?
faqs.answer: The Web Vitals guidance calls for Largest Contentful Paint within two and a half seconds, Interaction to Next Paint at 200 milliseconds or less, and Cumulative Layout Shift at or below one tenth, at the 75th percentile of loads. On a shop, the hero file should be cropped for the phone so the object paints first and the button does not jump.

faqs.question: What should a phone product page show before the story?
faqs.answer: The object, the name, the price shape, and the main limits: shipping, returns, make time. Variants need labels, not color alone. A sticky purchase action is reasonable if it does not cover the price.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
A consumer brand mobile website is how most shoppers who do not know you yet will judge the brand. The first screen still has to show the object clearly and offer a way to see the product. Design that screen at phone width. A desktop composition can add room later. It should not decide the order.

The visit is often one-handed, in daylight, between a recommendation and a decision to stay or leave. The page has to finish the introduction under those conditions.

## The first screen, at thumb width

Put the object on the first view, large enough to name without pinching. Put one plain sentence under or beside it. Put the link to the product on that same view, with a target a thumb can hit. If the link slips below the first view, the phone page is a poster of a brand the shopper still cannot enter.

Nielsen Norman Group's research on [how long people stay](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/how-long-do-users-stay-on-web-pages/) gives you about 10 seconds before many people leave, and less text than you hoped they would read. On a phone the screen holds fewer elements, so the object and the path consume the seconds. A logo animation, a newsletter wall, and a manifesto consume the same seconds and do not show the product.

Type has to work in daylight. A thin face in pale gray on a photograph will vanish outdoors. Solid ground, dark text, a button that looks like a button. The poetic name can be present. The plain noun has to be readable. "Mug" can live in the sentence even if the product name is more delicate.

The button uses shop words. See the mug. Shop outerwear. The same words as the header. A phone visit has no extra patience for a synonym invented by the campaign.

## What the wide layout tries to steal

Desktop designs like a cinematic crop, a column of brand essay, and a menu that only fits when the window is large. On a phone those choices become a tiny slice of the object, a wall of prose, and a hidden drawer. Review the phone as its own page. Decide what the wide layout may add once the narrow page already works.

Horizontal product rows are a common theft. On a desktop they show four objects. On a phone they become a swipe the shopper never finds, so one product stands in for the brand by accident. Stack them, or show two with a visible control. The range is too important to hide in a gesture nobody was taught.

Video headers are another theft. They delay the object and punish a weak connection. If you keep motion, put a still of the product and the link first. Let the video be a choice. Autoplay with sound is an argument with the shopper in a public place. You will lose that argument.

Pop-ups that cover the object to ask for an email are a third theft. The errand was to see the product. Ask for an address after they have seen it, or in the footer. A discount that hides the thing is a manifesto about the discount. The product was supposed to lead.

## Speed, stability, and the picture

A phone on an ordinary connection will expose a heavy image. Core Web Vitals, as [web.dev lays them out](https://web.dev/articles/vitals), describe three parts of the experience. Largest Contentful Paint should occur within 2.5 seconds for a good result. Interaction to Next Paint should be 200 milliseconds or less. Cumulative Layout Shift should stay at 0.1 or less. Judge at the 75th percentile of loads, on mobile and on desktop.

For a product brand, Largest Contentful Paint is often the hero photograph. That file should be cropped and compressed for the phone, not delivered as a print file the browser shrinks. The button should not jump when a font arrives. A layout shift that moves "See the product" at the moment of a tap is how a shopper opens the wrong story and concludes the shop is clumsy.

Load the page on a phone and watch what paints first. If the first paint is a full-bleed landscape and the object arrives late, the priority is the manifesto's priority. If the object and the link arrive together and stay still, the page is serving the decision.

Hanabi builds this kind of site in Next.js, React, TypeScript, and Tailwind, and hosts with the studio's usual path on Vercel. The stack is worth naming only because a simple first screen stays fast. Effects are optional. The product link is not. Motion, if you use it, should not be the thing the phone waits on.

## The product page on a small screen

The product page is where the phone visit either completes or dies. Show the object in a tap-through set: the clear frame, the detail, the use. Make the set obvious. Dots that are too small, or a swipe with no affordance, hide the detail you needed the shopper to see. The price shape sits under the name, before a long story. Included, not included, make time, returns in one line.

Variants have to be tappable. Color swatches need labels, not color alone, so the choice is perceivable and so a person does not guess. Size as a list they can read. An out-of-stock variant stays visible and marked, so the price logic does not disappear along with the stock.

Add to bag should stay reachable. A sticky action on a phone is reasonable when the page is long. It should name the product. A sticky bar that covers the price is a failure of the bar. The price and the action belong together. Shipping surprises belong on this page, not only at the last step of checkout. A careful brand can still lose the order by introducing a new number after the shopper thought they understood.

Forms for made-to-order should be short. Measurements you truly need. A note on the wait. Confirmation on the page. A shopper typing with one thumb will abandon a form that resets.

## Touch, glare, and motion

Buttons need space so a thumb does not open a journal while reaching for the product. The spirit of operable content applies in daylight and rain, not only in an audit. The control has to be usable by the person you claim to want.

If something moves, it should show a product fact. A fabric detail opening is a fact. A paragraph that fades in line by line delays the price. Honor reduced motion. The still version should contain the same object and the same link, not a diminished brand. Reduced motion is a preference, and it is also a courtesy on a shaky train.

Glare will erase pale type. Test the first screen outdoors once, with the brightness at a normal setting. If you cannot read the noun, darken the type or put it on a solid field. Five minutes outside will do more for the brand than another round of desktop kerning.

Checkout, if it is yours, should feel like the same shop. The object thumbnail, the price you already showed, and the same voice. A checkout skinned by a default that does not match is a new brand at the worst moment. If a platform constrains you, match type and spacing as far as the platform allows, and keep the numbers consistent.

Run the first screen on a cheap phone, not only on the device in the design review. The object should still be nameable, the type should still be readable, and the link should still sit in the first view. If the page only works on a large new phone, it only works for part of the people you are trying to meet. Compress the hero until the object paints first. A slow landscape with the product somewhere inside it is the manifesto winning on a loading bar.

Keep the same product name in the button that the product page uses as its heading. A shopper who taps "See the coat" and lands on a page titled with a poetic line has to re-identify the object. That re-identification is a stutter. Remove it.

State the shipping region in the first product view on the phone, in one line, if you cannot ship where many of your visitors live. A shopper who only learns the limit at payment has spent their attention on an object they cannot have. The line can be quiet. It has to be present. A brand that is honest early feels more careful, which is the tone the photographs were trying to earn.

## When they still need a person

Some phone visits should reach a human. A fault, a wholesale question, a size that sits between two charts. The contact path has to say what happens next, how soon, and what to have ready, and it should not outrank the product. That path is [a contact path for a consumer brand](/blog/a-contact-path-for-a-consumer-brand).
